imperial.name: Mushroom

actions.text:
Start kit

Any month indoors if the kit’s conditions can be maintained.

methods.text:
Start the kit 

Stand the kit out of direct sunlight. Check when to add the casing. Some kits are ready straight away, while others need a few days for white threads to spread across the compost.

Add the casing 

When it’s ready, spread the casing loosely over the surface and keep it damp. Follow the kit instructions for temperature and whether to leave the lid on.

panelBlocks.text: Fancy making your own growing medium?

If you don’t want to buy a complete kit, oyster mushrooms will grow in clean straw from a friendly farmer or bedding straw from a pet shop. You will need a suitable PVC box or strong plastic bag to keep the medium contained and clean. A spawn supplier can recommend a suitable wrapping or container and may be able to supply it. Buying commercial spawn is always recommended – you need to be certain what type of mushrooms you are growing!

Put the straw in a heatproof container and pour boiling water over it. Follow the supplier’s advice on how much water to use and how long to soak it. Let the straw cool to room temperature and drain off the excess water.

With clean hands, layer the damp straw and spawn in your chosen wrapping or container. Follow the supplier’s advice on air holes. Once white threads have spread through the straw, give the mushrooms fresh air and indirect daylight.
Button and chestnut mushrooms. These have more exacting requirements and usually require additional ingredients for the medium, such as manure and gypsum. Again, your spawn supplier can advise.

Mushrooms grow in prepared mushroom compost away from direct sun. Fresh ready-spawned kits in bags, buckets or boxes are the simplest route to small crops while outdoor beds are quiet. Check the start-by date and begin promptly: pre-started kits may already be largely colonised. Follow the supplier’s stages, casing and temperatures.

Fancy making your own growing medium?

If you don’t want to buy a complete kit, oyster mushrooms will grow in clean straw from a friendly farmer or bedding straw from a pet shop. You will need a suitable PVC box or strong plastic bag to keep the medium contained and clean. A spawn supplier can recommend a suitable wrapping or container and may be able to supply it. Buying commercial spawn is always recommended – you need to be certain what type of mushrooms you are growing!

Prepare the straw

Put the straw in a heatproof container and pour boiling water over it. Follow the supplier’s advice on how much water to use and how long to soak it. Let the straw cool to room temperature and drain off the excess water.

Add the oyster spawn

With clean hands, layer the damp straw and spawn in your chosen wrapping or container. Follow the supplier’s advice on air holes. Once white threads have spread through the straw, give the mushrooms fresh air and indirect daylight.

Button and chestnut mushrooms. These have more exacting requirements and usually require additional ingredients for the medium, such as manure and gypsum. Again, your spawn supplier can advise.

Key risks
Mushroom flies

Small flies around the trays may be the first sign. Their larvae feed in the compost and can damage young mushrooms.

Contaminating moulds

Contaminating fungi can discolour mushroom substrate or distort and decay developing mushrooms.

Poor cropping

Slow colonisation or stalled cropping may result from unsuitable temperatures, moisture or ventilation.

VEGETABLE GUIDES

OTHER

Start with prepared mushroom compost.

A fresh ready-spawned kit is the simplest route for small quantities.

Keep conditions steady.

Avoid direct sun, temperature extremes and waterlogged casing.

Soil & preparation
Kit mushrooms grow on prepared mushroom compost. For a small crop, buy a kit with the spawn already growing through the compost.
Kits usually come with a separate bag of casing. This is the loose top layer that holds moisture and helps the mushrooms form.
Starting a mushroom kit
Check for white threads
Spread the casing
Start the kit 

Stand the kit out of direct sunlight. Check when to add the casing. Some kits are ready straight away, while others need a few days for white threads to spread across the compost.

Add the casing 

When it’s ready, spread the casing loosely over the surface and keep it damp. Follow the kit instructions for temperature and whether to leave the lid on.

Looking after the crop
Follow the kit temperatures for spawn growth and cropping. Keep the kit ventilated and out of direct sun.
Colonising compost gives off heat. Check the supplier’s temperature range to avoid overheating.
Many button kits crop at 61–64°F; follow the supplier’s range. Water casing carefully to keep lightly moist, never saturated.
Harvesting & storage
Pick before the veil opens for closed buttons, later for open caps. Flushes alternate with rests; timing and duration depend on kit and conditions.
Twist buttons gently to lift without much disturbance. Trim dirty bases and remove broken remnants; refill holes with suitable casing if the kit advises.
After the last crop, compost healthy spent substrate or use as soil improver. Weather first near seedlings/salt-sensitive plants: mushroom compost can contain high soluble salts. Start with fresh prepared material.
Keep the casing moist between flushes. Once cropping ends, empty, wash, rinse and dry reusable containers.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Mushroom flies	Small flies appear; larvae damage mushrooms or compost.	Use clean equipment, exclude flies and remove spent or infested material.
Contaminating moulds	Unusual coloured mould or misshapen, decaying mushrooms.	Isolate affected kits; ask the supplier and discard contaminated material.
Poor cropping	Spawn runs poorly or cropping stalls.	Check kit temperature, moisture and airflow; avoid sun and saturation.
Final tips

Use fresh kits and check the supplier’s start-by date rather than storing them indefinitely.

Grow from identified cultivated spawn; do not treat an unknown mushroom appearing nearby as part of the crop.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
67

This guide covers cultivated button and chestnut mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), grown
Preparing compost from raw ingredients needs controlled composting and conditioning; other mushroom species need different substrates and conditions.
Button mushrooms need prepared mushroom compost, not garden soil. Buy fresh spawned compost or a kit. Commercial compost often uses straw, manure and gypsum, processed before spawning.
edits.after: Kit mushrooms grow on prepared mushroom compost. For a small crop, buy a kit with the spawn already growing through the compost.

edits.before: Home preparation needs initial composting plus controlled pasteurisation and conditioning to remove ammonia. Looks or a fixed number of turns cannot prove readiness; use a complete tested method and suitable equipment.
After colonisation, button mushrooms need a moist casing layer. Follow the kit’s casing material and timing; keep moist, never saturated. Other species may not need casing.
